text: And here is a boy, no more than twelve, carrying a bucket of water that is much too heavy for him, which is why he is carrying it with both arms, and which is why he is walking in the careful, straight-legged way of a person whose whole body is committed to not spilling something. Nobody stops him. Nobody helps him. Everyone has carried a bucket like that, once. Now, there is one thing we should look at, and then we will leave the camp alone. Near the middle of the camp, the ground has been cleared, and flattened, and reinforced with beams. There is a ring of men around that cleared ground, but they are not standing in ranks. They are sitting, or lying, or leaning, the way people do near a thing that is too big to look at for very long. In the middle of the clearing, there is the shape we saw from the wall. It is a cannon. But "cannon" is too small a word. This is a thing cast in bronze, in one piece, so long that a man cannot reach from one end to the other with both arms wide. It rests on a wooden cradle, and the cradle rests on wheels, and the wheels are as tall as men. It is the largest gun anyone in this camp has ever seen. Possibly the largest gun anyone anywhere has ever seen. And it is not ready. That is the part of the story that is easy to forget, and that we should not forget tonight. The great gun is not a magic object.

It is a machine, and machines are tired, and this one has been fired so many times that its mouth has begun to split, and so the men have been working on it , with rings of iron, and ropes, and hot metal, and the patience of people who have only one idea and cannot afford a second. They will finish it. Probably tonight. Probably before the light. And then, in the morning, it will speak. But not yet. Not for a few hours. Let us walk back, away from the clearing, to the edge of the camp, where the light of the fires stops, and the ground goes dark, and the grass begins again. Here, there is a man on his own, sitting on a stone, looking out at nothing in particular. He is not a soldier. Or he is, but he has stopped being one for the evening. His helmet is on the ground beside him. His hands are empty. He is looking at the city. At the lights along the wall. He has been looking at them for some time. You might think he is thinking about tomorrow. But look at his face, if you can see it in the dark, and you will see that he is not thinking about tomorrow at all. He is thinking about a town he knew, when he was young. You can tell by the way his mouth has gone a little soft at the corners. He is thinking about a street, and a door, and a person who used to stand in that door. He will never see it again. He knows this. He is not sad about it, exactly.

He is simply there, with it, the way you sit with a fire on a cold night. Let us leave him. Let us go back, across the ditch, past the quiet stone, and in through the gate, and up the tower stairs, and back to the window with the open shutter. Tomorrow, everything will change. But it is not tomorrow yet. It is still tonight. And tonight, both cities are still here.
